title: Corresponding squares
summary: For every square of one king, the square the other king must be on: the method behind opposition, triangulation and blocked pawn endings.
part.doors.title: Two doors, one king
part.doors.summary: Separated key squares and the first pairs: where each king needs to be.
part.number.title: Numbering the squares
part.number.summary: The method: from the doors backwards, every white square gets a black partner.
part.opposition.title: Opposition is a special case
part.opposition.summary: Rösch–Mast, 1995: pairs on the same rank; and Grigoriev's triangulation.
part.lasker.title: Lasker and Reichhelm, 1901
part.lasker.summary: The most famous position of the method: a king walk along the first and second ranks.
part.defend.title: The method also defends
part.defend.summary: Every square of the black king has an answer; and the recap of the lesson.
step.t_doors: White to play and win. A study by Grigoriev, 1924. The pawns are locked and the black king seems close to everything. Where does the white king need to get in, and why does the black king, on f4, arrive late?
step.t_doors.hint1: The white king has two doors, far apart: e2 or f2, from where it supports the advance d4, and a3 or b3, from where the c3-pawn falls.
step.t_doors.hint2: On f4, the black king guards neither e2 nor f2. On f3 it would guard both.
step.trebuchet: You know the trebuchet: each king attacks the other's pawn, and whoever has the move loses his own. Two squares, d5 and f4, that correspond: if my king is on one, the black king needs to be on the other, with me to move. A single pair. Corresponding squares are the same idea with many pairs: for every square of my king, the square the black king needs to be on. Whoever can number the pairs knows, from far away, where the king must go.
step.doors: Now put the black king on f3 and give White the move. From f3 it guards e2 and f2, the door on the right. If I go to d1, eyeing the door on the left, it answers e3: still guarding e2 and f2, and one step closer to b4, the square that shuts a3 and b3. If I go back to e1, it goes back to f3. Those are the first two pairs: d1 with e3, e1 with f3. With the black king on the partner square and me to move, I do not get in. With the black king off it, as on f4, I get in at once.
step.d_enter: The study position, with the black king on f4. Watch the door open, and then the rest of the technique.
step.d_enter.m1: 1.Ke2. From f4 the black king guards neither square of the door; 1.Kf2 worked just as well.
step.d_enter.m2: The black king retreats to hold the centre.
step.d_enter.m3: 2.Ke3: the king supports the advance d4.
step.d_enter.m4: Face to face, to stop the advance.
step.d_enter.m5: 3.d4, with check. The pawn steps out and my king stays beside it.
step.d_enter.m7: 4.Kd3, the only move: it attacks the c3-pawn and faces the black king. Any other square lets Black come back.
step.d_enter.m8: To avoid losing the c3-pawn for nothing, the black king steps back, still facing mine.
step.d_enter.m9: 5.Ke4: the king gains space and prepares d5.
step.d_enter.m11: 6.d5, with check. The black king has to pick a side.
step.d_enter.m13: 7.Kd4, facing it, the only move. The black king is tied to the pawn.
step.d_enter.m15: 8.Kc5. Now the white king threatens two things: to fetch the c3-pawn via b4, and to push the d5-pawn. The black king cannot hold both.
step.enter: White to play and win. Your king is already on a square of the door, e2, but it is your move and it cannot stand still.
step.enter.hint: The other square of the door is next to it. Any other move draws: the retreats to the first rank let the black king take f3 or e3, and d4 locks everything.
step.enter.done: That's it. 1.Kf2 kept the door, and the black king has to leave f4. Then come 2.Ke3 and 3.d4: the technique from the demonstration.
step.t_number: White to play and win. Now the black king is on d5 and yours on c1, far from the doors. 1.Kb1, 1.Kd1 or 1.d4: only one wins. Number the squares before you choose.
step.t_number.hint1: The doors are the same: e2 and f2, a3 and b3. Which white squares threaten to get in, and which black square answers each one?
step.t_number.hint2: d1 and e1 threaten e2; e3 and f3 guard e2 and f2. c1 is next to d1 and b1; d4 is next to e3 and c5. Every white square has a black partner.
step.t_number.hint3: Count, from d5, the partner squares the black king can reach in one move. One of the three white squares has a partner out of his reach.
step.count: The method starts from the doors. On the right, d1 and e1 threaten e2; e3 and f3 guard e2 and f2. Which goes with which? d1 is one step closer to the other door, so d1's partner is the black square one step closer to it: e3. That leaves e1 with f3. Now walk left. c1 is next to d1 and b1; the black square next to e3 and c5 is d4: c1 with d4. b1 is next to c1 and a2; c5 is next to d4 and b4: b1 with c5. a2 threatens a3 and b3; b4 guards both: a2 with b4. And a1, next to a2 and b1, goes with b5, next to b4 and c5. Six pairs: every square on the first rank from a1 to e1 has a black partner. From f1 to the right there is no partner: from there the white king enters on e2 or returns to e1 whenever it wants.
step.rule: The rule follows from the pairs. If every square of mine has a partner and the black king is always on it, it holds. So my move is to go to the square whose partner it cannot reach in one move. Here the black king is on d5, which is nobody's partner: from d5 it reaches c5 and d4, but not e3. 1.Kd1!, whose partner is e3. 1.Kb1? has partner c5, and it goes there: draw. 1.d4? locks everything: draw. Counting the squares means this: seeing who runs out of answers first.
step.d_number.m1: 1.Kd1, whose partner is e3. From d5 the black king cannot get there.
step.d_number.m2: It goes to c5, the partner of b1. But I am not on b1, and it is my move.
step.d_number.m3: 2.Ke2: the door. From c5 nobody guards e2.
step.d_number.m7: 4.d4, with check, as in the first part.
step.d_number.m9: 5.Kd3: it attacks c3 and faces the black king. It is the position you have already seen win.
step.numberMove: White to play and win. The black king is on f3, yours on f1. Two moves: at each step of his, the partner square.
step.numberMove.hint: f3 is the partner of e1. Then e3 is the partner of d1.
step.numberMove.done: Perfect. 1.Ke1 against f3, 2.Kd1 against e3, and now it is the black king that has to leave: when it goes to d4, the e2 door opens (3.Kc1, the partner of d4, would also win, only more slowly).
step.t_rosch: White to play and draw. Rösch–Mast, 1995. The black king wants to reach e3, e2, e1 or f3: from any of them it wins. Only one move holds.
step.t_rosch.hint1: Your king needs to guard e3, e2 and e1 at the same time, and f3 as well.
step.t_rosch.hint2: From f2 the king guards all four squares. Afterwards, at each step of the black king down the d-file, the opposition on the same rank.
step.rosch: Here the key squares belong to Black: e1, e2, e3 and f3. The pairs are easy to see: d3 with f3, d2 with f2, d1 with f1. Kings on the same rank, two squares apart, with Black to move: that is the horizontal opposition. The opposition you learned is just the case where the partner squares line up. And the black king on e4 has partner f2: the only square from which I answer d3 with f3 and d2 with f2.
step.d_rosch.m1: 1.Kf2, the only move. From f2 I guard e1, e2, e3 and f3, all the squares the black king wants.
step.d_rosch.m2: The black king comes to d3, threatening e2 and e3.
step.d_rosch.m3: 2.Kf3: the partner square. Horizontal opposition, with Black to move.
step.d_rosch.m4: Then d2, threatening e1, e2 and e3.
step.d_rosch.m7: 4.Kf1. There is no step below. The black king can go back and try again; the answer is always the same: the partner square. Draw.
step.triangle: Triangulation is a case of the method too. In this study by Grigoriev the doors are e2, e3 and d4. The partner of d2 is f3, of c3 it is e3, of c2 it is f4. Only b2 and b3 are as good for me as d2: they all have the same partner, f3. I have three squares with the same number and the black king has only one. I go round via c2, b3 and b2, and it cannot keep up: it is the triangle you already know, seen through corresponding squares.
step.roschMove: White to play and draw. Rösch–Mast in the mirror: the black king wants d1, d2, d3 or c3. Hold.
step.roschMove.hint: Only one square guards d1, d2, d3 and c3 at the same time. Afterwards, at each step of the black king down the e-file, the opposition on the same rank.
step.roschMove.done: Well done. 1.Kc2, and then c3 against e3, c2 against e2, c1 against e1. The black king does not get in. Draw.
step.t_lasker: Lasker and Reichhelm, 1901. White to play and win. Ten pieces, everything locked, and the white king in the corner. It has two doors: b5, on the queenside, and h5, on the kingside. What is the first move?
step.t_lasker.hint1: 1.Ka2 and 1.Kb2 only draw: the black king answers b8 or a8 and always stays one step from its answers.
step.t_lasker.hint2: Look for the square whose partner is c7. From a7, the black king cannot reach c7 in one move.
step.laskerKeys: Two doors again, further apart. On the left, c4 threatens to enter on b5 and win the a5-pawn; the partner of c4 is b6. On the right, the king goes via e3, f3, g3 and h4 to h5, and the f5-pawn falls; the black king needs to be on d7 or d8 when I reach e3. Between the doors, the pairs the line needs: b3, d3, b1 and d1 have partner c7; c3 and c1 have partner b7; d2 has partner c8; c2 has partner b8. The black king on a7 is on nobody's partner square, and the move is the square whose partner it cannot reach: 1.Kb1.
step.d_lasker: The white king's walk, move by move.
step.d_lasker.m1: 1.Kb1, the only winning move. The partner of b1 is c7, and from a7 the black king cannot reach c7.
step.d_lasker.m2: The black king chooses b7, the partner of c3 and c1.
step.d_lasker.m3: 2.Kc1: the partner of b7, with Black to move. They have to leave.
step.d_lasker.m4: To c7, the partner of b1 and d1.
step.d_lasker.m5: 3.Kd1: the right partner again, and again it is their move.
step.d_lasker.m6: The black king goes to d8, eyeing the door on the right.
step.d_lasker.m7: 4.Kc2, whose partner is b8. From d8 you cannot reach b8.
step.d_lasker.m8: Black settles on c8, the partner of d2.
step.d_lasker.m9: 5.Kd2: the partner of c8, and it is their move.
step.d_lasker.m10: To d7, still eyeing the right.
step.d_lasker.m11: 6.Kc3, partner of b7. From d7 you cannot reach b7.
step.d_lasker.m13: 7.Kd3: the partner of c7, for the third time with Black to move. Now the answers have run out: if the black king goes to b6 or b7, I get in on the right; if it goes to d7 or d8, I get in via c4 and b5.
step.d_lasker.m15: 8.Ke3: the race to h5. The black king needed to be on d7 or d8, and it is on b6.
step.d_lasker.m18: The black king reaches d7, but I have already gone past.
step.d_lasker.m23: 12.Kh5, and Black is in zugzwang: the king has to leave f5, I get in on g5 and the pawn falls. A pawn up and the king inside, the rest is counting.
step.laskerMove: White to play and win. Make Lasker's first two moves.
step.laskerMove.hint: The partner of b1 is c7, and the black king on a7 cannot get there. Then answer b7 with its partner square.
step.laskerMove.done: That's it: 1.Kb1 and 2.Kc1, the two only moves. From there it is the walk of the demonstration, pair by pair, until the door opens.
step.defend: The method also defends. Here the black king will try two roads: the middle, via e7 and e6, and the edge, via g7, g6 and g5, with the h5-pawn behind it. Your king needs to stay at the right distance from both. The pairs: f8 with g2, e7 with h3, f7 with g3, g7 with f3, g6 with f4, h6 with f5. The odd one is the first: against the black king in the middle of the eighth rank, the white king steps back to g2, the only move that holds. From there it answers e7 with h3 and g7 with f3, and never runs out of answers.
step.defendMove: White to play and draw. Answer each square of the black king with its partner.
step.defendMove.hint: Against f8, g2. Against e7, h3. Against f7, g3.
step.defendMove.done: That's it. 1.Kg2, 2.Kh3 and 3.Kg3: every square of the black king had its answer. As long as it stays that way, it does not get in.
step.recap: Three rules to take with you. First: start from the doors, the key squares; the squares next to them form the first pairs. Second: a square next to two numbered squares is the partner of the square on the other side next to the same numbers; that is how the pairs walk backwards. Third: on your move, go to the square whose partner the other king cannot reach; if it always can, it is a draw, and that is how the method defends. Opposition and triangulation are cases of this method: in the opposition the partners line up; in triangulation you have more squares with the same number than your opponent.
step.finish: Now play to the end. The black king is on b5, yours on c1, and it is your move. Find the square whose partner it cannot reach, get in through the door and convert.
key.grigoriev: Grigoriev, 1924: the white king has two entry doors, far apart, and the black king can't guard both at once.
key.method: The method at work: for every square of the black king there is one right square for the white king. White goes to the only one the black king can't answer.
key.roschMast: Rösch against Mast, 1995: White draws by answering every step of the black king with the matching square, always beside it.
key.triangle: A study by Grigoriev: the white king has three squares that answer the same square of the black king, and so it can lose a tempo. This is triangulation seen through corresponding squares.
key.lasker: The method's most famous position, by Lasker and Reichhelm, 1901: the white king takes a long, patient walk until it forces its way in, and White wins.
key.defend: The method works in defence too: for every step of the black king, the white king answers with the matching square, and the draw is safe.
history: In some pawn endings the kings stand facing each other, away from the pawns, in a waiting dance: whoever puts a foot wrong loses. The opposition explains the simple cases, but not all of them. For the rest there is the method of corresponding squares: for every square the enemy king can go to, there is one right square for your king. It's an ending that looks like a matter of patience and is really a matter of calculation, and even books have got it wrong. The most famous position dates from 1901, composed by Emanuel Lasker, then world champion, and the American Gustavus Reichhelm. And there's a lovely curiosity: in 1932 the painter Marcel Duchamp, who was also a chess master, wrote a whole book on this subject with Vitaly Halberstadt.
practice: Now the real ending: the black king on b5, yours on c1, and it is your move. Find the square whose partner it cannot reach, get in through the door and win. Pick your pace and go.
ex.e01: White to play and win. King and pawn against king: the simplest pairs of the method.
ex.e01.hint: The partner of c6 is c8. From e8, can the black king get there?
ex.e01.solution: 1.Kc6! The partner of c6 is c8, and from e8 the black king cannot reach c8. After 1...Kd8, 2.d7!, the black king has to go to e7 and 3.Kc7 takes the pawn through. 1.Kd5? allows 1...Kd8, the pair with me to move, and draws; 1.d7+? draws too.
ex.e02: White to play and win. Doubled pawns on the b-file, and the black king in front of them. Where does the white king go?
ex.e02.hint: c4 and b6 are a pair: whoever arrives first, with the other able to answer, has to step back. Wait on a square next to c4.
ex.e02.solution: 1.Kd4! (1.Kd3 and 1.Kb3 also win): c4 and b6 are the pair, and the white king waits beside it. After 1...Kb6, 2.Kc4!, and it is the black king that has to leave; if 1...Kc7, 2.Kc5. 1.Kc4? at once allows 1...Kb6!, and it is you who steps back: draw. 1.b6? draws as well.
ex.e03: White to play and draw. The a6-pawn is stuck, and the black king wants a7.
ex.e03.hint: 1.Kb5? takes the king towards c6, but 1...Ka7! and the a6-pawn falls first. Look for the partner square of b8.
ex.e03.solution: 1.Kb4!, the partner of b8; nothing else holds. After 1...Ka8, 2.Kc4 (or 2.Ka4), and when the black king returns to b8, 3.Kb4 again. 1.Kb5?, 1.Ka3?, 1.Kb3? and 1.a7+? lose.
ex.e04: White to play and win. A study by miguel_angel_jodraza. A pawn up, but the white king is in the corner and the black one close to everything. Only one move wins.
ex.e04.hint: On the f- and g-files the distant opposition rules: g1 with g7, f1 with f7, g2 with g8 and g6, f2 with f8 and f6. On the d- and e-files, next to the pawns, the pairs vanish. Stay on the right files.
ex.e04.solution: 1.Kg1!, the distant opposition on the g-file (1.Kg2? allows 1...Kg8 or 1...Kg6; 1.Kh2? and 1.c5? draw as well). After 1...Kf7, 2.Kf1!, the partner of f7. If the black king runs to e7, 3.Kg2 (or 3.Kg1): from e7 it cannot get back to g8, g6 or g7, and the opposition is yours for good. 3.Ke1? or 3.Ke2? behind it draw: on the e-file the pair does not hold.
ex.e05: White to play and draw. A study by Strategically_Endgam. The black king wants to reach e2 and e3, next to the f3-pawn, and has the advance ...e4 up its sleeve. Only one move holds, and it is not the one it seems.
ex.e05.hint: The pairs here lie on the same rank: e1 with g1, e2 with g2, e3 with g3; d1, d2 and d3 with h1, h2 and h3. Which square is the black king on now?
ex.e05.solution: 1.Kh1!!, the partner of d1. Then, at each step of the black king, the partner on the same rank: Kg1 against e1, Kg2 against e2, Kg3 against e3; Kh2 against d2. 1.Kg3?, 1.Kf1?, 1.Kf2? and all the others lose: the black king reaches e1 or d2 with White to move, and gets in.
step.t_defend: White to play and draw. Now you defend. The black king will choose a road: through the middle, via e7 and e6, or along the edge, via g7 and g6, with the h5-pawn behind it. Which square of the white king answers both roads?
step.t_defend.hint1: 1.Kf2, 1.Kf4 and 1.Ke4 lose: on each of them the black king picks the road your king cannot reach. The right square is a retreat, and not the one it seems.
ex.e06: White to play and win. A study by Strategically_Endgam. The black king guards b6, c7 and c5. Only one move wins.
ex.e06.hint: The white king goes round through the corner: the pairs are a6 with c6 and a7 with c7. The spare tempo of the a3-pawn decides who has the move; spend it at the right moment.
ex.e06.solution: 1.Ka6! (1.a4?, 1.c5?, 1.Ka4? and 1.Kb4? draw). After 1...Kc6, 2.a4! The spare tempo, spent now, leaves the black king to move (2.Ka7? allows 2...b5 and draws). After 2...Kc7, 3.Ka7!, the partner of c7; after 3...Kc6, 4.Kb8 (or 4.Ka6, 4.Ka8), and the white king reaches b7 and takes the pawns. If 1...Kb8 right at the start, 2.Kxb6.
